slides.title: Endpoints: Where Security Meets Hardware
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: NIST SP 800-128 defines an endpoint as any device connecting to an enterprise network; Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) tooling specifically targets this layer.

Analogy: If the network is a fortress's walls and gates, the endpoint is the door of an individual room inside, the wall can be perfect and a single unlocked door still lets someone in.

Exam tip: When a scenario names a specific device (laptop, camera, router), the exam is usually testing endpoint-layer vocabulary, not network-layer vocabulary.
bullets: Endpoint: any device used directly by a person/process, laptops, phones, servers, IoT
The place where network-security abstractions (firewalls, tunnels) terminate at real hardware
Most frequently attacked layer because humans and software directly interact with data there

content_blocks: An endpoint is any device that sits at the 'end' of a network connection and is used directly by a person or process, laptops, desktops, smartphones, servers, and IoT devices like cameras or thermostats. Endpoints are where humans and software actually interact with data, which makes them the most frequently attacked layer of any network.

This topic examines the device itself as the target: what makes an operating system, firmware, or an embedded controller inherently exploitable, and how adversaries convert a single compromised endpoint into a foothold for the rest of the network.

slides.title: Attack Surface: Counting the Doors
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Formalized by Manadhata & Wing (2011), 'An Attack Surface Metric,' IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering. Codified as NIST SP 800-53 control family CM (Configuration Management).

Analogy: A house with ten unlocked windows is riskier than one with two, even if both have the same locked front door.

Misconception: A bigger, more feature-rich device is not inherently 'more secure', every added feature is usually added surface.
bullets: Attack surface: the complete set of entry/exfiltration points on a system
Every open port, running service, installed app, user account, physical interface counts
More surface = more places for something to go wrong
Endpoint security = minimizing surface (hardening) + assuming breach (defense in depth)

content_blocks: The academic frame for endpoint vulnerability is attack surface, the complete set of points where an unauthorized user could try to enter or extract data from a system. Every running service, open network port, installed application, and default account on a device is a potential entry point.

Endpoint security, as a discipline, is the practice of systematically minimizing that surface (hardening) while simultaneously assuming that some component of it will eventually be breached (defense in depth), and building detection capability around that assumption.

slides.title: Two Questions to Classify Any Malware Sample
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: NIST SP 800-83 Rev. 1, 'Guide to Malware Incident Prevention and Handling,' is the canonical federal reference for malware taxonomy.

Misconception: Students try to memorize malware types as a flat list instead of asking these two questions, which makes scenario questions hard to answer.

Exam tip: Always separate 'how it got in / how it spreads' from 'what it does once inside' when labeling a scenario.
bullets: Question 1: How does it get onto the device? (infection vector)
Question 2: How does it propagate/persist once there? (behavioral classification)
These are independent dimensions, a single sample can satisfy several labels at once
Malware = any program intentionally written to damage, disrupt, spy on, or gain unauthorized access

content_blocks: Malware (malicious software) is the primary payload category deployed once an endpoint vulnerability has been located. Understanding malware requires separating two independent questions students frequently conflate: how does it get onto the device (the infection vector, phishing, drive-by download, USB, network exploit) and how does it propagate and persist once there (the behavioral classification).
A single sample of malware is often described using several classifications simultaneously, because they describe different dimensions of behavior rather than mutually exclusive categories.

slides.title: Virus vs. Worm vs. Trojan: Infection Mechanisms
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Cohen, F. (1987), 'Computer Viruses: Theory and Experiments,' formally defined computer viruses as self-replicating code. The 1988 Morris Worm was the first internet worm and prompted the creation of the first CERT.

Analogy: A virus is like a biological virus needing a host cell; a worm is autonomous like a self-driving vehicle; a trojan is the Greek myth, a gift that hides an attacker inside.

Exam tip: If a scenario says 'no user interaction was required and it spread across the network on its own,' that is a worm, not a virus.
bullets: Virus: attaches to a host file, requires human execution to activate and spread
Worm: self-replicating, network-aware, spreads with zero user interaction
Trojan: disguised as legitimate software, relies entirely on deception, does not self-replicate
Key distinction: worms are autonomous, viruses are parasitic, trojans are deceptive

slides.title: Virus vs. Worm vs. Trojan: Infection Mechanisms
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Cohen, F. (1987), 'Computer Viruses: Theory and Experiments,' formally defined computer viruses as self-replicating code. The 1988 Morris Worm was the first internet worm and prompted the creation of the first CERT.

Analogy: A virus is like a biological virus needing a host cell; a worm is autonomous like a self-driving vehicle; a trojan is the Greek myth, a gift that hides an attacker inside.

Exam tip: If a scenario says 'no user interaction was required and it spread across the network on its own,' that is a worm, not a virus.
content_blocks: A virus requires a host file and human execution to activate and propagate; it inserts its code into legitimate executables or documents (macro viruses). A worm is self-propagating and network-aware, it does not need a host file or user interaction, autonomously scanning for and exploiting vulnerable services. A trojan is disguised as legitimate software; unlike a virus or worm, it does NOT self-replicate, relying entirely on social engineering to convince the user to run it once.

slides.title: Ransomware and Rootkit: Objectives, Not Vectors
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS) groups like LockBit and BlackCat/ALPHV lease encryption toolkits to affiliates for a cut of the ransom. FBI IC3 2023: reported ransomware losses exceeded $59.6 million. Kernel-mode rootkits (ring 0) and firmware/bootkit rootkits (e.g., LoJax, 2018) can survive a full disk wipe.

Misconception: Paying a ransom does not guarantee data recovery or that exfiltrated data won't still be leaked.

Exam tip: 'Hides from the OS itself, even Task Manager shows nothing wrong' is the rootkit signature phrase.
bullets: Ransomware: encrypts victim data, extorts payment for the decryption key
Double extortion: exfiltrate data first, threaten to publish even if backups exist
Rootkit: gains AND conceals privileged ('root') access, hides from OS-level tools
Kernel-mode and firmware/bootkit rootkits are especially hard to detect and remove

content_blocks: Ransomware encrypts a victim's files (or locks their system) and demands payment, usually cryptocurrency, for the decryption key. Modern groups also exfiltrate data first and threaten to publish it even if the victim has backups, a tactic called 'double extortion.' A rootkit is a toolkit designed to gain and maintain privileged access while actively hiding its own presence, from the file system, running-process lists, and even the OS kernel itself.

slides.title: Privilege Escalation: From Foothold to Full Control
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: MITRE ATT&CK Tactic TA0004. CWE-269, 'Improper Privilege Management,' catalogs common root causes. Principle of least privilege formalized by Saltzer & Schroeder (1975); codified as NIST SP 800-53 control AC-6.

Analogy: A hotel keycard that only opens your room's door (least privilege) vs. a master key an attacker must steal or forge (escalation).

Exam tip: Distinguish vertical (up the privilege ladder) from horizontal (sideways to a peer's data) escalation explicitly if asked.
bullets: Privilege escalation: exploiting a flaw/misconfig to gain rights beyond what was granted
Vertical escalation: standard user → admin/root
Horizontal escalation: accessing another equally-privileged user's data
Least privilege means attackers almost never land with full access, they must escalate

slides.title: Privilege Escalation: From Foothold to Full Control
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: MITRE ATT&CK Tactic TA0004. CWE-269, 'Improper Privilege Management,' catalogs common root causes. Principle of least privilege formalized by Saltzer & Schroeder (1975); codified as NIST SP 800-53 control AC-6.

Analogy: A hotel keycard that only opens your room's door (least privilege) vs. a master key an attacker must steal or forge (escalation).

Exam tip: Distinguish vertical (up the privilege ladder) from horizontal (sideways to a peer's data) escalation explicitly if asked.
content_blocks: Privilege escalation is the deliberate exploitation of a flaw or misconfiguration to convert an initial low-privilege foothold into administrative control. Because most endpoint operating systems apply the principle of least privilege to newly-created accounts by default, attackers who compromise a low-value account (e.g., via phishing) must still escalate before they can install persistent malware, disable security tooling, or move laterally to higher-value systems.

slides.title: IoT Devices: A Uniquely Exploitable Endpoint Class
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: NISTIR 8228, 'Considerations for Managing IoT Cybersecurity and Privacy Risks,' identifies IoT devices as uniquely difficult to secure because they often cannot run traditional endpoint agents due to limited compute resources.

Misconception: 'It's just a camera, not a computer', any IoT device with an OS and network stack is a full endpoint from an attacker's perspective.

Exam tip: IoT-specific answers should mention BOTH resource constraints AND default-credential/patch-cadence problems.
bullets: IoT: embedded, network-connected everyday devices (cameras, thermostats, locks, sensors)
Manufacturers often prioritize cost/time-to-market over security engineering
Limited compute resources often prevent running traditional AV/EDR agents
Infrequent or nonexistent firmware updates + undocumented default credentials

content_blocks: An increasingly significant category of endpoint is the Internet of Things (IoT) device: an embedded system, typically running a stripped-down Linux distribution, with limited compute resources, infrequent (or nonexistent) firmware update mechanisms, and, critically, factory-set default credentials that are rarely changed by end users or even documented for customers to change.

slides.title: Default Credentials at Internet Scale
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Shodan (founded by John Matherly, 2009) indexes metadata about every publicly reachable device rather than web pages. The Mirai botnet source code (leaked 2016) hardcoded 61 common IoT default credential pairs.

Analogy: Instead of trying every doorknob on a street by hand, the attacker uses a directory of which doors are unlocked, published for them in advance.

Exam tip: 'Attackers scanned the entire internet for a specific open port/service' is a Shodan-style reconnaissance signature.
bullets: Default admin passwords: factory-preset username/password, meant to be changed, rarely is
Mirai's leaked source code hardcoded 61 common IoT default credential pairs
Attackers use mass scanners (Shodan, masscan) to fingerprint device banners at scale
Matching hosts are fed into automated credential-stuffing scripts, no manual targeting

slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Shodan (founded by John Matherly, 2009) indexes metadata about every publicly reachable device rather than web pages. The Mirai botnet source code (leaked 2016) hardcoded 61 common IoT default credential pairs.

content_blocks: To understand why default administrator passwords remain such an effective attack vector at internet scale, examine how automated scanning and credential-stuffing tools operate. Adversaries do not manually test devices one at a time; they run mass internet scanners such as Shodan or custom masscan-based tooling that fingerprint device banners on common ports, then feed matching hosts into automated credential-stuffing scripts.

slides.title: Reading a Compromise: Auth Log Walkthrough
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: CWE-272, 'Least Privilege Violation,' and MITRE ATT&CK T1548.001 (Setuid and Setgid) formally document the SUID persistence technique.

Misconception: Students sometimes think the login attempt count matters more than the timing, it's the sub-second spacing between failures that signals automation, not just the number of failures.

Exam tip: Always narrate a log left to right: vector → success → escalation → persistence/payload, in that order.
bullets: 4 rapid Failed password attempts from same IP = scripted brute force, not human typing
5th attempt Accepted password for admin = credential-stuffing success
sudo chmod 4755 on /bin/busybox = SUID escalation for persistent root access
cron job downloads mirai.arm = enrollment into a Mirai-family IoT botnet

slides.title: The SUID Bit: A Persistence Trick
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: CWE-272 and MITRE ATT&CK T1548.001 document this technique formally.

Analogy: It's like an employee badge that was set to always open the CEO's office regardless of who is holding it, the door checks the badge's permission level, not the person.

Exam tip: 'SUID bit set on a binary' in a log is a high-severity persistence indicator, not just an access event.
bullets: SUID (Set User ID): program runs with the FILE OWNER's privileges, not the invoker's
chmod 4755 sets SUID (leading '4') + rwxr-xr-x permissions
If root owns the binary, ANY user who executes it temporarily runs as root
Classic embedded-Linux persistence: attacker regains root anytime by invoking that binary

slides.title: The SUID Bit: A Persistence Trick
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: CWE-272 and MITRE ATT&CK T1548.001 document this technique formally.

Analogy: It's like an employee badge that was set to always open the CEO's office regardless of who is holding it, the door checks the badge's permission level, not the person.

Exam tip: 'SUID bit set on a binary' in a log is a high-severity persistence indicator, not just an access event.
content_blocks: The SUID bit is a special Unix/Linux file permission flag that causes a program to run with the file owner's privileges rather than the privileges of the user who launched it. If a program owned by root has the SUID bit set, any user who executes it temporarily runs with root privileges for that execution. Attackers who gain limited access frequently set the SUID bit on a shell or utility binary as an easy way to regain root access later, even after their original credentials are revoked.

slides.title: Telnet: Plaintext Remote Administration
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: RFC 854 defines Telnet (1983). NIST SP 800-53 control CM-7 (Least Functionality) flags Telnet as an unnecessary and dangerous open service that should be disabled by default.

Misconception: A closed network is not automatically a safe one to run Telnet on, any device on that same local segment, including a compromised one, can sniff it.

Exam tip: Port 23 open = immediate red flag; pair it with 'SSH (22) disabled' for full credit on hardening questions.
bullets: Telnet (1969, RFC 854): transmits ALL data, including credentials, unencrypted
Frequently left enabled on IoT firmware for factory diagnostics, never disabled before shipping
Any attacker on the network path can harvest credentials directly from the wire
SSH created specifically to replace Telnet by adding encryption

slides.title: Telnet: Plaintext Remote Administration
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: RFC 854 defines Telnet (1983). NIST SP 800-53 control CM-7 (Least Functionality) flags Telnet as an unnecessary and dangerous open service that should be disabled by default.

Misconception: A closed network is not automatically a safe one to run Telnet on, any device on that same local segment, including a compromised one, can sniff it.

Exam tip: Port 23 open = immediate red flag; pair it with 'SSH (22) disabled' for full credit on hardening questions.
content_blocks: Telnet is a very old remote-login protocol that transmits all data, including the username and password used to log in, as unencrypted plaintext over the network. Because Telnet transmits credentials as cleartext, any attacker positioned on the network path, or simply scanning for open port 23, can harvest valid logon credentials directly from the wire without needing to guess them at all.

slides.speaker_notes:
Context: Mirai means 'future' in Japanese. Its source code was published on Hack Forums by author 'Anna-senpai' in September 2016, paradoxically causing a proliferation of Mirai variants once it became public.

Exam tip: Note that no individual device was targeted, this was mass, automated, indiscriminate scanning.
content_blocks: In September 2016, source code for the Mirai botnet malware was released, revealing a program purpose-built to compromise IoT devices, home routers, IP cameras, and DVRs, that had never had their factory-default Telnet credentials changed. Mirai's scanning engine continuously probed random IP ranges for open port 23, attempted its hardcoded credential list, and upon success, downloaded and executed a small ARM/MIPS binary that enrolled the device into a command-and-control botnet.

content_blocks: On October 21, 2016, an army of Mirai-infected devices launched a massive Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attack against Dyn, a major DNS infrastructure provider. Because Dyn's DNS services resolved domain names for a large portion of the internet, the attack caused widespread outages for major platforms for several hours. The attack was traced to an estimated 100,000+ compromised IoT devices, none of which had been individually targeted, they were simply scanned, found vulnerable via default credentials, and conscripted en masse.

slides.title: Why Mirai Worked: Scale, Not Sophistication
slides.speaker_notes:
Misconception: Students sometimes assume a large-scale attack must involve sophisticated, novel exploitation. Mirai used no zero-day, only unchanged factory defaults at massive scale.

Exam tip: Scale can substitute for sophistication as an attack multiplier, be ready to explain this trade-off in a free response.
bullets: No individual camera owner was 'hacked' in a targeted sense
Manufacturers shipped hundreds of thousands of near-identical devices with the same weak defaults
Virtually none of those owners ever logged in to change the password
A single vulnerability class, multiplied across enough devices, becomes a strategic weapon

A single vulnerability class, multiplied across enough devices, becomes a strategic weapon.

slides.title: Case Study: WannaCry, A Worm-Ransomware Hybrid
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: EternalBlue exploited CVE-2017-0144 in Windows SMBv1, developed by the NSA and leaked by the Shadow Brokers in April 2017, one month before the attack. Attributed to North Korea's Lazarus Group.

Exam tip: This is the canonical example of a scenario needing BOTH a propagation label and an objective label.
bullets: May 2017: infected 200,000+ computers across 150 countries within days
Crippled parts of the UK's NHS, causing appointment/surgery cancellations
Propagation = worm (EternalBlue SMBv1 exploit, zero user interaction)
Objective = ransomware (AES+RSA encryption, ~$300 Bitcoin demand per machine)

slides.title: Case Study: WannaCry, A Worm-Ransomware Hybrid
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: EternalBlue exploited CVE-2017-0144 in Windows SMBv1, developed by the NSA and leaked by the Shadow Brokers in April 2017, one month before the attack. Attributed to North Korea's Lazarus Group.

Exam tip: This is the canonical example of a scenario needing BOTH a propagation label and an objective label.
content_blocks: In May 2017, the WannaCry ransomware worm infected an estimated 200,000+ computers across 150 countries within days, notably crippling parts of the UK's National Health Service. WannaCry combined two elements this topic classifies separately: it was a worm in its propagation (using EternalBlue to spread laterally with no user interaction) and ransomware in its objective (encrypting files with AES and RSA and demanding Bitcoin).

slides.title: WannaCry's Root Cause: Unpatched Endpoints
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: EternalBlue's underlying vulnerability, CVE-2017-0144, carries a CVSS v2 base score of 9.3, indicating critical severity.

Exam tip: 'A patch existed but was not applied' is the single most common root cause tested in patch-management free-response scenarios.
bullets: Microsoft released patch MS17-010 a full month before the attack
Large population of enterprise/government machines never applied it
Many were running unsupported Windows XP and Windows 7 installations
A security researcher's discovery of an unregistered kill-switch domain slowed the spread

slides.title: WannaCry's Root Cause: Unpatched Endpoints
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: EternalBlue's underlying vulnerability, CVE-2017-0144, carries a CVSS v2 base score of 9.3, indicating critical severity.

Exam tip: 'A patch existed but was not applied' is the single most common root cause tested in patch-management free-response scenarios.
content_blocks: The rapid, global spread of WannaCry was made possible entirely by unpatched endpoints: Microsoft had shipped a patch closing the EternalBlue vulnerability a full month prior, but a large population of enterprise and government machines, many running unsupported Windows XP and Windows 7, had not applied it. WannaCry was eventually slowed by a security researcher who discovered and registered an unregistered domain referenced in the malware's code, acting as an unintentional 'kill switch.'

slides.title: Labeling Hybrid Malware Correctly

quiz.question: A sample spreads by exploiting an unpatched network service with no user click required, then quietly copies files to an attacker-controlled server without altering or locking anything on the victim machine. Which is the correct classification?
choices: A worm with a spyware/exfiltration objective
A virus with a ransomware objective
A trojan with a rootkit objective
A worm with a ransomware objective
quiz.answer: A worm with a spyware/exfiltration objective
quiz.explanation: Autonomous network-based spread with no user interaction is a worm's propagation mechanism; quietly stealing data without altering/locking it is a spyware/exfiltration objective, not ransomware.

slides.speaker_notes: Exam tip: Structure hybrid-malware answers as two clauses: '[propagation mechanism] used to deliver a [objective] payload.'
bullets: Classifications describe different dimensions: propagation mechanism vs. payload objective
WannaCry = 'a ransomware payload delivered via wormable propagation'
On the exam, identify BOTH the propagation mechanism AND the payload objective
Forcing a single label loses partial credit on free-response questions

slides.title: Eliminating Default Configurations
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: NIST SP 800-53 control CM-7 directs organizations to disable all services not explicitly required for business operations, Telnet almost never meets this bar.

Exam tip: 'Verified through automated scanning' beats 'checked manually' as an answer whenever the question asks about scale/reliability of a control.
bullets: Mandatory credential rotation before any device is provisioned onto production network
Telnet service disablement, turn the daemon off entirely, don't just change its password
Verified through automated configuration compliance scanning (CIS-CAT, OpenSCAP)
NIST SP 800-53 control CM-7 (Least Functionality) mandates disabling unneeded services

Example rules: disable SMBv1, set minimum password length to 14

Context: CIS Benchmarks map directly to the CIS Critical Security Controls and are frequently referenced alongside NIST SP 800-53.

Exam tip: Naming a specific framework (CIS Benchmarks, NIST SP 800-53) rather than saying 'follow best practices' earns more credit on free response.
content_blocks: The CIS Benchmarks published by the Center for Internet Security provide device- and OS-specific hardening checklists that organizations apply as a baseline configuration standard prior to deployment. Combined with NIST SP 800-53's CM and SI control families, these frameworks formalize the process of reducing attack surface as a repeatable, auditable procedure rather than an ad hoc decision left to individual administrators.

slides.title: IoT-Specific Regulatory Controls
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: SB-327 is sometimes called the first IoT-specific cybersecurity law in the United States, drafted directly in response to incidents like Mirai/Dyn.

Exam tip: This is the strongest available answer to 'what single control best prevents another Mirai-scale event', regulation at the manufacturer level, not user education.
bullets: Manufacturers, not end users, control security posture at point of manufacture
California SB-327 (2020): unique per-device default passwords OR forced setup password change
UK Product Security and Telecommunications Infrastructure Act, similar requirement
Directly targets the root cause exploited by Mirai

slides.title: IoT-Specific Regulatory Controls
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: SB-327 is sometimes called the first IoT-specific cybersecurity law in the United States, drafted directly in response to incidents like Mirai/Dyn.

Exam tip: This is the strongest available answer to 'what single control best prevents another Mirai-scale event', regulation at the manufacturer level, not user education.
content_blocks: Recognizing that manufacturers, not end users, control the security posture at the point of manufacture, regulators have begun mandating security-by-design requirements. California's SB-327 (effective 2020) and the UK's Product Security and Telecommunications Infrastructure Act require that IoT devices sold in those jurisdictions either use unique per-device default passwords or force a password change during initial setup, directly targeting the root cause exploited by Mirai.

slides.title: Patch and Vulnerability Management
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: CVSS is maintained by FIRST.org. EternalBlue's CVE-2017-0144 carries a CVSS v2 base score of 9.3.

Exam tip: Cite a CVSS score threshold and a specific tool (Nessus/Qualys) when asked to describe a formal patch management program.
bullets: A released patch is only effective if deployed, WannaCry's central lesson
CVSS (0.0–10.0): rates vulnerability severity to determine patch urgency
CVSS 9.0+ ("Critical") often requires patching within 24–72 hours per policy
Validated through automated vulnerability scanning (Nessus, Qualys), not spreadsheets

slides.title: Defense in Depth for Endpoints: Three Layers

quiz.question: An organization disables Telnet on all new IoT deployments, sets up SIEM alerts for repeated failed logins, and has a documented process to isolate any host showing a SUID escalation event. Which defense-in-depth layer is MISSING from this description?
choices: None, all three layers are present
quiz.answer: None, all three layers are present
quiz.explanation: Disabling Telnet = preventive; SIEM alerts on failed logins = detective; documented isolation process = corrective/responsive. All three layers are explicitly named.

slides.speaker_notes: Exam tip: Even under time pressure, write one sentence per layer rather than a long paragraph on only one layer, partial credit is layer-counted, not depth-counted.
bullets: Preventive: disable unnecessary services, change default credentials, apply patches
Detective: log and alert on failed authentication and privilege escalation events
Corrective/Responsive: isolate the compromised host, rotate exposed credentials
Graders award partial credit PER LAYER, naming all three maximizes score

Context: This is the same pattern-recognition skill tested directly on log-excerpt free-response questions, just automated at scale in a real Security Operations Center (SOC).

Exam tip: If asked to design a detection rule, describe both the pattern (rapid failures, same source) AND the correlated follow-up event (success, then privilege change).

slides.title: Synthesis: The Endpoint Compromise Kill Chain
slides.speaker_notes:
Context: This mirrors the Cyber Kill Chain (Lockheed Martin, 2011) introduced in Unit 2, applied specifically to the endpoint layer.

Exam tip: When a free-response question gives a full incident narrative, map each sentence onto one of these four stages before writing your answer, it structures your response automatically.

Exam tip: When a free-response question gives a full incident narrative, map each sentence onto one of these four stages before writing your answer, it structures your response automatically.
content_blocks: Synthesizing the whole topic into one chain: an attacker's tooling scans the internet for an exposed insecure default (open Telnet, unpatched SMB); gains initial access via credential-stuffing or exploiting an unpatched vulnerability; escalates and persists using techniques like the SUID bit or a rootkit; then executes on its objective, whether that's botnet enrollment for DDoS (Mirai), file encryption for extortion (WannaCry), or quiet data exfiltration. Breaking the chain at any single link, patch the service, remove default credentials, detect the escalation, stops the entire attack.

items.text: Identify the classes of computing device in an environment — servers, workstations and laptops, mobile handsets, network appliances, and the embedded and industrial controllers with no screen or keyboard — and account for how each differs in what it can run and how long its vendor supports it.

Determine, from what an incident actually did, which family of malicious software was involved: whether it needed a host file and a person, whether it moved between machines unaided, whether it arrived disguised as legitimate software, and whether its purpose was extortion, concealment, surveillance, or theft.

Explain the route from a device weakness to the concrete harm an adversary can produce with it, naming each step from the initial vulnerability to data lost, hardware damaged, operations halted, or records destroyed.

Assess the weaknesses present on a fleet of devices and document them so the findings can be acted on — each scored for likelihood and impact, ranked against the others, and recorded where the decision to fix or accept it can later be audited.

big_idea.text: An unpatched device is a house whose lock design was published in a public catalog. The vulnerability becomes common knowledge long before most owners get around to changing what's on their door.
